analysis.one_liner: Delays stricter smog limits, doubles the time between air-quality reviews, and shields states from penalties for missing goals.
analysis.headline: The House passed a bill delaying the 2015 smog standard 229–199 on July 18, 2017, but the Senate never voted on it, so the stricter ozone rule stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2015 EPA rule set a tighter limit on ground-level ozone, the main ingredient of smog, which comes mostly from vehicle exhaust, refineries, chemical plants, and power generation. This bill pushed back every deadline for implementing that rule by three to eight years, stretched the review cycle for all air-quality standards from five years to ten, barred EPA from even starting its next ozone review before late 2025, let cost and technological feasibility count against a tighter health standard, and exempted states from federal penalties for failing to clean up smog. It passed the House on a mostly party-line vote but died in a Senate committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had become law, refineries, chemical plants, power plants, and other large emitters in smoggy areas would have gained years of delay before they had to cut emissions: designations of which areas must clean up would not be final until 2025, state cleanup plans would not be due until 2026, permits for new facilities filed before designation would be exempt from the new standard, extreme ozone areas would skip backup contingency measures, and states could escape fees and sanctions by blaming pollution from outside the area or from vehicles. States that found the 2015 deadline hard to meet would also have gained breathing room.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large industrial polluters in smoggy areas

how_it_helps.text: The bill delays implementation of the 2015 ozone standard until at least 2025 for designations and 2026 for state cleanup plans, instead of the original timeline.
It stretches the review cycle for all national air-quality standards from five years to ten, and bars EPA from completing its next ozone review before October 26, 2025.

It lets EPA treat technological feasibility as a secondary consideration when setting a health standard, and requires the agency to weigh economic feasibility in state cleanup plans for smog and soot, rather than standards being set on health grounds alone.

It exempts states from federal sanctions or fees for missing attainment deadlines if they show the excess pollution came from outside the area, an exceptional event, or mobile sources beyond state control, and it removes the requirement for contingency measures in extreme ozone areas.
It exempts certain preconstruction permit applications completed or noticed before final area designations from having to meet the 2015 standard.

analysis.who_pays: People who breathe the smog would pay: residents of ozone-polluted areas, especially children with asthma, older adults, and people with lung disease, would be exposed to air the EPA had already determined at the existing standard was unhealthy. That means more asthma attacks, missed school and work days, and higher medical costs for years longer than under the 2015 rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of smoggy areas, especially asthma sufferers

drawbacks.text: Every year of delay extends the period in which areas fail to meet a health standard EPA set in 2015, keeping populations exposed to ozone levels the agency had already linked to respiratory harm.

Allowing cost and technological feasibility to weigh against the health standard, and letting states escape penalties by attributing pollution to outside sources or mobile sources, weakens the enforcement mechanism that made the Clean Air Act's cleanup deadlines effective.

Supporters argued the 2015 standard's implementation timeline was unrealistic for states and that industry faced large compliance costs; the counterargument is that the bill answered a cost problem by shifting it onto public health rather than by providing resources, and the bill authorizes no additional funds for states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real point on the supporters' side: states and permit applicants genuinely lacked implementing guidance when the 2015 rule was issued, and the bill does require EPA to publish implementation rules at the same time as any new standard. But the bill's main effect is not better guidance — it is pushing the date cleaner air arrives years into the future, halving how often standards get reviewed, and removing penalty pressure from states and emitters. The compliance-cost savings for industry are the public-health costs borne by people in smoggy areas, and the bill offers them nothing in return.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote in July 2017, but the Senate sent it to its environment committee, which never acted on it before Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Pete Olson on February 1, 2017 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The subcommittee forwarded it 12–8 and the full committee reported it as amended on a 29–24 vote in June and July 2017.
All five Democratic amendments offered on the floor — from Reps. Castor, Tonko, Beyer, Polis, and McNerney — were rejected on July 18, 2017.
A Democratic motion to send the bill back with an instruction to block the law if EPA's science advisers found it would worsen health impacts for uninsured Americans failed 191–235 (Roll 390).
The bill passed the House 229–199 (Roll 391), with 225 of 239 voting Republicans in favor and 188 of 194 voting Democrats opposed.
The Senate received the bill on July 19, 2017 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
Because the bill never became law, the 2015 ozone standard and its original implementation timeline remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residents of ozone-polluted areas came out ahead: the stricter 2015 smog standard and its cleanup deadlines stayed in force because the Senate never acted. Industry's bid for years of delay and penalty relief failed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People breathing cleaner air kept the stricter standard

industries.note: Major stationary ozone sources that would have gained years before final nonattainment designations, state cleanup plans, and permit reviews under the 2015 standard, plus exemption for permits filed before designation. The savings come from delaying emission cuts in areas the EPA already found unhealthy.
Would have faced ozone and particulate cleanup requirements later and with an economic-feasibility escape hatch, keeping older plants running longer at the public's expense in respiratory health.

New and modified facilities would have avoided the stricter 2015 standard through the preconstruction permit exemption, and states could have avoided fees and sanctions by attributing excess pollution to sources outside the area.

Agencies struggling with the 2015 deadlines would have gained years of compliance time and a requirement that EPA issue implementing guidance with each standard; in exchange they lose the federal penalty pressure that funds and enforces cleanup. The bill authorizes no new money for the work.
